name: Surgerymaxxing

lead: Surgerymaxxing is looksmaxxing community shorthand for improving appearance mainly through surgery, often several procedures over time. Typical items discussed include rhinoplasty, eyelid surgery, jaw (orthognathic) surgery, facial implants, fat transfer and hair transplants.

The appeal is that surgery can change bone structure, proportions and soft tissue in ways that topical or lifestyle changes cannot. Individual procedures have decades of clinical literature behind them; the strategy of stacking many of them has mostly forum before-and-after threads.

paras: Members describe researching individual procedures, comparing surgeons and clinics (including abroad in Turkey or Korea), planning an order of operations, and sometimes consulting about how the changes fit together so the face looks harmonious. Recovery time and cost are discussed alongside results.

Every operation carries general surgical risks such as infection, bleeding, nerve injury, scarring and unsatisfactory or irreversible results, and clinical sources link strong preoccupation with appearance to body dysmorphic disorder, in which surgery often does not resolve distress. Community threads also raise 'uncanny' results from changing one feature in isolation, and travel-surgery complications.

web.title: Looksmaxxing: why people are hammering their faces and getting height surgery in the quest for love

chain: Pick procedures that target specific features (nose, eyes, jaw, hair)
Surgery alters bone, soft tissue or hairline directly
angle.text: Surgery changes facial structure and features directly, which proponents see as the route to results that grooming or skincare cannot reach. People typically plan procedures feature by feature and sometimes in stages, aiming for a balanced overall result.

lead: Surgerymaxxing is a term from looksmaxxing communities for using cosmetic and facial surgery, often several procedures in sequence, as the main way to change how one looks. It belongs to 'hardmaxxing', the invasive end of looksmaxxing, as distinct from non-invasive 'softmaxxing' such as skincare, grooming and fitness [1].

The procedures discussed most often are rhinoplasty, eyelid surgery (blepharoplasty, canthal work and so-called 'hunter eyes'), chin and jaw implants, jaw surgery such as Le Fort I maxillary advancement and bimaxillary osteotomy, fat transfer and hair transplantation [2][3][4]. People who pursue it say it is the one route that alters underlying bone and proportions, which is how a series of operations is expected to raise perceived attractiveness and, in many accounts, social attention [2].

Plastic and maxillofacial surgery are long-established medical fields with extensive clinical literature on individual operations [5][4]. The combined, multi-operation approach is documented mainly through forum before-and-after threads, travel-surgery guides, and surgeons' commentary in the news, which describes patients arriving with checklists of procedures drawn from looksmaxxing content [3][6].

paras: The word joins 'surgery' to the looksmaxxing suffix '-maxxing' (maximising). It describes a plan in which operations, rather than skincare, fitness or grooming, do most of the work of changing appearance. Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing places cosmetic surgery such as jaw surgery and rhinoplasty under hardmaxxing, alongside other invasive or off-label measures [1].

The common features are a feature-by-feature approach (nose, eyes, chin, jaw, hairline), an expectation that more than one operation will be involved, and a focus on skeletal change. Posters frequently refer to results in terms of looksmaxxing rating scales and to 'ascending' from one tier to another [2][7].

Rhinoplasty and blepharoplasty are two of the most common cosmetic surgeries overall; Wikipedia's figures for 2020 put rhinoplasty at about 15 percent and blepharoplasty at about 14 percent of cosmetic surgical procedures in the United States [5]. In looksmaxxing threads they are joined by canthoplasty and 'hunter eye' surgery aimed at the eye shape, fat transfer for the midface or under-eye area, and hair transplantation for the hairline [2].

Jaw surgery is the centre of much of the discussion. Orthognathic surgery was developed to correct jaw discrepancies such as overbite, underbite and receding chin, to treat sleep apnoea and to improve facial proportion; it includes bilateral sagittal split osteotomy of the lower jaw, Le Fort I osteotomy of the upper jaw and genioplasty of the chin [4]. Operating on both jaws is commonly called bimaxillary surgery, or 'bimax' in forum shorthand [2]. Wikipedia reports initial healing of roughly 2 to 6 weeks and bony remodelling over a further 2 to 4 months, with temporary numbness from inferior alveolar nerve injury a recognised complication [4].

Other posts describe more specialised work, including an AMA thread by a user describing a modified orbital box osteotomy with implants [8]. Surgeons quoted in the press list chin, jawline, lip, nose and hairline surgery, bimaxillary osteotomy and Le Fort I advancement among the operations young patients now ask about [3].

Looksmaxxing as a whole grew out of 2010s message-board culture, including PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, and reached a wider audience on TikTok in the 2020s [1]. Surgery has been part of the hardmaxxing vocabulary from the start; Wikipedia notes that maxillofacial surgery is frequently discussed [1].

On looksmax.org, 'surgerymaxxing' appears as thread titles for results galleries, planning threads and travel guides, and the AMA format lets patients answer questions about their operations [2][9][7][8]. Press coverage from 2023 described men on forums weighing overseas limb-lengthening and facial procedures, and a 2026 UT Southwestern commentary by plastic surgeon Christine Stiles described looksmaxxing as part of a wider online culture that is sending young men toward bimaxillary osteotomy, Le Fort I advancement, rhinoplasty and blepharoplasty [6][3].

Proponents argue that facial bone structure and proportions largely determine attractiveness and that surgery is the only tool that changes them. A widely shared thread presents a poster's account of more attention from others after six procedures, including bimaxillary surgery, rhinoplasty, a hair transplant, eyelid surgery and fat transfer [2]. Results-sharing threads collect before-and-after photos as motivation, which posters call 'lifefuel' [7].

A second strand of discussion concerns harmony. Posters argue that the face is a system in which each bone relates to the others, so altering one part can produce an 'uncanny' result, and they discuss planning the order of operations to avoid it [10][11][12]. One thread titled 'surgerymaxxing is cope' argues that isolated changes cannot recreate a naturally balanced face [10].

A third strand is cost and access. A guide on looksmax.org presents South Korea as comparatively inexpensive because of intense clinic competition and notes that operating-room CCTV is mandatory there, contrasting it with Turkey [13]. Threads also discuss small, staged plans over a summer or a year [9] and ask why very wealthy people do not appear to use surgery more [14].

Discussions describe researching each procedure, comparing surgeons and clinics (including abroad), sequencing operations over months or years, and allowing for recovery time [13][9]. Members share consultation experiences, recovery photos and complication stories, including threads documenting results they regard as poor [14][7].
Clinical guidance for patients in this situation, as stated by surgeons, centres on consulting a board-certified plastic surgeon for impartial advice and realistic expectations before committing [3].

Medical sources list complications of cosmetic surgery including hematoma, nerve injury, infection, scarring and unsatisfactory results [5]. Orthognathic surgery carries reported infection rates of up to 7 percent and some risk of lasting numbness [4].

Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a preoccupation with perceived flaws, is more common among people seeking cosmetic surgery than in the general population: Wikipedia cites about 2 percent of Americans against about 15 percent of patients seen by cosmetic surgeons and dermatologists, and a large meta-analysis estimates about 24 percent among people seeking plastic surgery [5][15]. Reviewers report that surgery often does not relieve BDD distress, and treatment for the disorder is generally cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRIs, with surgeons and psychiatrists encouraged to screen candidates together [15].

Australian surgeons and counsellors interviewed in 2023 warned that overseas hospitals may not meet local standards, described 'surgery ghosting' in which a different surgeon performs the operation, and said marketing can recast ordinary variation as a defect [6]. Stiles, writing in 2026, described a risk of cycles of corrective procedures and noted that social media content often looks more flattering than real life [3].

Within the community, critics raise the 'uncanny' result problem and share cases they consider failures [10][14]. Posters treat this largely as a planning question, and a minority treat it as a reason not to operate [10][12].

No studies found on surgerymaxxing as a multi-procedure strategy. Individual procedures such as rhinoplasty, blepharoplasty and orthognathic surgery each have their own clinical literature, which is described in Wikipedia's overviews of plastic surgery and orthognathic surgery [5][4].

The practice appears in results threads, travel-clinic guides and debates over whether surgery is the endpoint of 'ascension' [7][13][14]. It is often paired with discussion of hard-to-reverse choices, since an operation cannot easily be undone, and with the rating-scale vocabulary that frames outcomes [2][1].

lore.intro: Surgerymaxxing is discussed both as the highest-impact route to a changed look and as a risky one that needs careful planning [2][10].

claims.claim: Surgery changes attractiveness more than any non-invasive method
Changing one feature at a time leaves an unnatural, disharmonious face
Overseas clinics (Korea, Turkey) make multi-surgery plans affordable
A well-planned sequence can be done in a staged way over months
Wealth and status are not enough without surgery

timeline.event: Simon Hullihen's case is cited as the first published jaw-surgery operation of the orthognathic type [4].
Jaw osteotomies develop; Hugo Obwegeser later popularises the sagittal split osteotomy of the lower jaw [4].
Harold Gillies develops facial reconstruction methods that Wikipedia calls the foundation of modern plastic surgery [5].
Looksmaxxing vocabulary, including hardmaxxing, develops on incel and PSL-style forums [1].
Looksmaxxing spreads on TikTok; surgery sits among the topics discussed [1].
SBS The Feed reports on men weighing overseas procedures and DIY practices, with Australian surgeons voicing concern [6].
UT Southwestern plastic surgeon Christine Stiles publishes a commentary on surgical and other risks of looksmaxxing for young men [3].
